## Runtime contract recommendations

Recommend these initial verbs: `inspect`, `query`, `propose`, `check`, `commit`, `resume`. Patch operations cover object creation/removal, transform changes, physical-property changes, region definition, border policy, and rule installation/removal. Keep the vocabulary extensible through versioned schemas. Do not expose arbitrary JavaScript evaluation or unrestricted renderer mutation.

Separate immutable author provenance from current commit authority. The service constructs full job context after authentication. Worker copies carry context for computation, never proof of identity. Result acceptance checks both the service-issued job and its assigned execution channel. An envelope ID is not a bearer permission.

Recommend all-or-nothing batches with revision preconditions. Start with explicit conflict rejection. Automatic merge requires proven independence and belongs in later refinement. A durable edit revision and simulation tick are separate values. Physical checks additionally bind their starting checkpoint. Define a final tick boundary where checked effects become accepted.

Use a versioned world document as the portable source. Use Rapier snapshots as pinned-runtime checkpoints. Use glTF/GLB for visual assets, not permissions, region rules, or the complete world format. Canonical hashing must specify ordering and numeric normalization. Reject NaN and infinity. Store integer revisions without JavaScript precision loss.

Recommend nonoverlapping axis-aligned region volumes initially. Explicit priority resolves deliberate overlaps. Border policy names allowed movement, rejected movement, and dimension transfer. Ordinary same-dimension crossings preserve pose and velocity. Transfers between dimensions declare coordinate and velocity transforms. Objects with joints transfer as an approved connected group or fail atomically. Destination readiness and permissions are preconditions.

A single Rapier world has a global gravity vector. Gravity scaling cannot express every regional vector. Regional gravity therefore requires controlled force application or distinct physics spaces. Bodies in distinct Rapier worlds do not automatically collide. Recommend shared clocks within interacting space, separate dimensions for incompatible clocks. Architecture must specify transfer behavior instead of implying seamless cross-engine contact.

Recommend fixed simulation steps of 1/60 second initially. This is a tunable engineering default, not measured capacity. Browser rendering follows requestAnimationFrame. Dedicated server simulation uses explicit step scheduling as physical time advancement, not state polling. Headless checks run a bounded number of steps. Queue and deadline events handle synchronization. Preserve project rules against timer-based rendering and repeated readiness checks.

The WASM bus should expose versioned messages, import allowlists, payload limits, bounded queues, and deterministic ordering. Default imports supply time as simulation ticks, seeded randomness, permitted queries, and proposed effects. Do not supply ambient network, filesystem, process environment, or arbitrary host functions. Validate memory declarations and module features before instantiation.

Native JavaScript WebAssembly APIs do not provide a portable instruction-fuel budget. Worker termination supplies a wall-clock deadline, not deterministic instruction accounting. Node worker resource limits exclude external buffers. Recommend a supervised process with operating-system memory limits for untrusted server modules, plus bounded WASM memory and message quotas. Browser execution remains a preview with worker deadlines. The server independently validates every accepted effect. A deterministic fuel mechanism remains an architecture choice requiring a focused proof before claiming instruction-budget enforcement.

## Evidence and limits

The [Rapier determinism guide](https://rapier.rs/docs/user_guides/javascript/determinism/) supports deterministic results with the same version, initialization, object order, and inputs. Arbitrary host math and extension behavior can break those conditions. Pin engine versions, step order, seed, and configuration. Bounded checks demonstrate declared assertions over a finite horizon. They do not prove arbitrary extension correctness.

The [Rapier snapshot guide](https://rapier.rs/docs/user_guides/javascript/serialization/) documents binary snapshots. The [scene query guide](https://rapier.rs/docs/user_guides/javascript/scene_queries/) supplies geometric perception. Neither replaces the portable semantic world document.

Two focused local experiments ran:

1. Node `22.18.0`: clone `Object.freeze({agentId:'author', runId:null})`, then change clone identity. Result: original frozen `true`, clone frozen `false`, original author unchanged, clone changed. This confirms that copied immutability cannot authenticate worker results. The [HTML structured-clone standard](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/structured-data.html#structuredserializeinternal) specifies reconstruction across realms.
2. Node `22.18.0`, Rapier `0.21.0`: create a dynamic sphere at y=10, gravity -9.81, timestep 1/60. Step 60 times, snapshot, restore, then advance both worlds 60 times. Snapshot size: 2,651 bytes. Final SHA-256 snapshot hashes matched. Final y: -9.660922050476074. Both worlds were freed. This establishes one local restore/replay path, not cross-browser determinism or performance.

Rapier was installed only in a temporary research directory. No runtime dependency or implementation was added to Metaform. Registry metadata was read directly with bounded network timeouts. No multiplayer benchmark, adversarial sandbox proof, browser parity test, or complete integration test ran.

- Crash after commit before acknowledgment. Retry after context cleanup. Recover outbox delivery after Metaform outage.
- Run infinite-loop, memory-growth, oversized-message, forbidden-import, and recursive-bus fixtures. Verify bounded termination and healthy authority.
- Profile application allocation, draw calls, frame-time median/p95/p99, simulation-step time, queue depth, and patch latency. Record hardware and fixture sizes. Performance targets require measured reference hardware before becoming acceptance thresholds.

Capacity recommendation for the first benchmark fixture: two browser clients, one agent, two regions, four streamed chunks, 100 dynamic bodies, and one extension. This fixture is a test scope, not a production capacity promise. Increase load only after correctness gates pass.

Architecture must settle storage transactions, hard sandbox enforcement, canonical schemas, border transfer details, durable receipt projection, and protocol compatibility. # Tasks

> Asynchronous task execution for long-running MCP operations

The [ext-tasks repository](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-tasks) contains the full specification and documentation for MCP Tasks.

> **[modelcontextprotocol/ext-tasks](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-tasks)**
>
> Full specification and documentation for MCP Tasks.

Not every tool call returns instantly. Some operations — CI pipelines, batch
processing, human approvals — take seconds, minutes, or longer. MCP Tasks let
servers return a durable handle instead of blocking, so clients can poll for
progress, provide input when needed, and retrieve the final result after
reconnecting.

## Why not just block?

You could hold the connection open until the work finishes. Tasks solve
problems that blocking cannot:

* **No long-lived connections.** Blocking ties up a connection for the duration
  of the operation. Many clients and transport intermediaries impose timeouts
  that make this impractical beyond a few seconds.
* **Crash resilience.** A task ID is a durable handle. If the client
  disconnects or restarts, it can resume polling with the same ID.
* **Progress visibility.** Tasks carry status metadata (`working`,
  `input_required`, `completed`, `failed`, `cancelled`) and optional status
  messages, giving clients visibility into progress.
* **Mid-flight interaction.** When a task needs input (e.g., an elicitation for
  user confirmation), it moves to `input_required` and surfaces the request.
  The client responds via `tasks/update` — no second connection or unsolicited
  server-to-client messages required.
* **Server-directed.** The server decides per-request whether to create a task.
  Clients opt in once via the extension capability and handle whichever result
  shape arrives. No per-tool warmup or per-request flag.

## How Tasks work

Tasks extend the standard request flow. When a server decides a request will be
long-running, it returns a task handle instead of the final result. The client
polls for completion.

1. **Capability negotiation.** The client includes
   `io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks` in its per-request capabilities. The server
   advertises the same extension in its own `server/discover` capabilities.

2. **Task creation.** In response to a supported request, the server returns a
   `CreateTaskResult` (identified by `resultType: "task"`) containing a `taskId`,
   initial status, TTL, and suggested polling interval. The task is durably
   created before the response is sent.

3. **Polling.** The client calls `tasks/get` with the `taskId`. The response
   carries the current status and, for terminal states, the final result or
   error.

4. **Mid-flight input.** If the task moves to `input_required`, the `tasks/get`
   response includes an `inputRequests` map with elicitations or other server
   requests. The client fulfills these via `tasks/update`.

5. **Completion.** When the status reaches `completed`, the `result` field
   contains what the original request would have returned synchronously. If the
   status is `failed`, the `error` field contains the JSON-RPC error.

6. **Cancellation.** The client can send `tasks/cancel` at any time.
   Cancellation is cooperative — the server acknowledges the intent but is not
   obligated to stop the work.

## When to use Tasks

Tasks are a good fit when your use case involves:

**Long-running operations.** CI pipelines, batch data processing, or model
training jobs that take minutes or hours.

**Human-in-the-loop workflows.** Approval gates, review steps, or any operation
that pauses for user confirmation. The task moves to `input_required` and the
client presents the request.

**External job systems.** If your server wraps an API that already uses job IDs
(cloud deployments, async APIs, queued work), return a task when you create the
job and resolve it when the job completes.

**Unreliable connections.** Mobile clients, intermittent networks, or
environments where connections drop. Task IDs survive disconnects.

**Batch processing.** Operations that process many items (bulk imports, mass
updates) where partial progress is meaningful. Status messages report progress.

## Task lifecycle

| Status | Meaning |
| - | - |
| `working` | The operation is in progress. |
| `input_required` | The server needs client input before continuing. See `inputRequests`. |
| `completed` | The operation finished. The `result` field contains the final output. |
| `failed` | A JSON-RPC error occurred during execution. The `error` field has details. |
| `cancelled` | The operation was cancelled (not always honored). |

`completed`, `failed`, and `cancelled` are terminal — once reached, the task's
state does not change.

## Notifications

Servers can push status updates via `notifications/tasks`. Clients opt
into these through the `subscriptions/listen` mechanism. Each notification
carries the full task state, eliminating the need for an extra `tasks/get`
round-trip.

Polling is the default. If a server supports notifications, clients can rely on
them instead of polling.

## Implementation guide

### For MCP clients

To consume task-augmented responses, your client must:

**1. Declare support**

Include the extension in its per-request capabilities:

```jsonc theme={null}
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "method": "...",
  "params": {
    // Other fields...
    "_meta": {
      // Other fields...
      "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities": {
        "extensions": {
          "io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks": {},
        },
      },
    },
  },
}
```

**2. Handle polymorphic results**

When issuing a supported request (e.g., `tools/call`), be prepared to receive
either the standard result or a `CreateTaskResult` with `resultType: "task"`.

**3. Poll for completion**

Call `tasks/get` with the returned `taskId`, respecting the `pollIntervalMs`
value. Continue polling until the task reaches a terminal status (`completed`,
`failed`, or `cancelled`).

**4. Handle input requests**

If the task status is `input_required`, read the `inputRequests` map, present
the requests to the user or model, and submit responses via `tasks/update`.

**5. Persist task IDs**

Store task IDs durably so polling can resume after a client crash or restart.

### For MCP servers

To return tasks from your server:

**1. Advertise support**

Include the extension in your `server/discover` capabilities:

```jsonc theme={null}
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "result": {
    // Other fields...
    "capabilities": {
      "extensions": {
        "io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks": {},
      },
    },
  },
}
```

**2. Check client capabilities**

Before returning a `CreateTaskResult`, verify that the client included the
extension in its per-request capabilities. Never return a task to a client that
did not declare support.

**3. Return CreateTaskResult**

When a request will be long-running, respond with `resultType: "task"` and a
`Task` object containing a unique `taskId`, initial status, `ttlMs`, and
`pollIntervalMs`. The task must be durably created before sending the response.

**4. Serve tasks/get**

Return the current task state on each poll. For terminal states, include the
`result` (on `completed`) or `error` (on `failed`) field.

**5. Handle tasks/update**

Accept `inputResponses` keyed to outstanding `inputRequests`. Acknowledge with
an empty result. Ignore responses for unknown or already-satisfied keys.

**6. Handle tasks/cancel**

Acknowledge cancellation requests with an empty result. Honor them when
possible, but cancellation is cooperative — the task may still reach a
non-`cancelled` terminal status.

## Client support

>
> MCP Tasks is an extension to the [core MCP specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest.md). Host

See the [client matrix](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/extensions/client-matrix.md) for extension support across
clients. Task support requires explicit opt-in from both client and server.

The Tasks extension is specified in the [ext-tasks repository](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-tasks). Worker lifetime and identity

- Each worker is a named, persistent, multi-skilled project agent.
- Workers retain their context across tickets.
- Completing one ticket does not terminate a worker while project work continues.
- Workers process messages from the system, user agent and peers.
- When all agents have finished and no new tickets have appeared, they leave the map and end their contexts.

Project agent skills

- There are no specialist agents or specialist-role registrations in the MCP server.
- Project agent skills reside in the expertise layer, attached through joins at the nodes where they apply.
- Workers inspect that layer as they navigate and dynamically load applicable skills.
- They use base map extension when introducing unmapped functionality.
- They use spec_enhancement when blocked by incomplete, ambiguous or flawed specifications.
- There is no additional knowledge-growth duty imposed on workers.

Facilitator and tickets

- The facilitator writes tickets for teams of two agents.
- Every ticket has a concise summary phrase.
- The facilitator chooses the work division and how checklist progress represents each agent’s contribution.
- The intended outcome is that both partners finish together.
- These responsibilities do not create role-based ticket-authoring permissions.

Planning and worksheet registration

The agent taking a ticket becomes its holder and coordinates that ticket:

1. Read the ticket and prepare an end-to-end completion plan.
2. Create and formally register its checklist or worksheet.
3. Allocate specific elements between the two agents.
4. Update its board entry with the planned elements.
5. Discover the applicable project agent skills through those elements.

The worksheet determines progress. There is no separate “finalizing” stage.

Partner selection and waiting

1. Inspect other agents’ current work, histories, ratings and Next entries.
2. Look for a suitable partner with no Next task listed.
3. Send a polite invitation describing the planned assignments.
4. Wait for acceptance.
5. Once accepted, register the partnership and the applicable checklist total as 0/N.

Invitations are resolved through conversation. An agent receiving competing offers can politely explain that it selected another offer. There is no automatic reservation rule or enforced first-come selection.

The holder plans in advance, then can go dormant while its accepted partner finishes their current work. The preferred behavior is to wake the waiting agent when that partner completes their current ticket.

There is no percentage threshold controlling this process.

Execution and progress

- Both agents execute their allocated work and communicate throughout execution.
- The holder tracks both contributions against the registered worksheet.
- Completed checklist items update the applicable board count.
- Completion percentage is calculated as:

  completed checklist items ÷ total checklist items × 100
- The facilitator’s ticket design determines whether the displayed count represents shared progress or an individual allocation.

- Ratings are numeric and cover multiple categories.

- Each partner critically rates the other partner’s completed contribution through the peer-rating MCP tool.

- Workers must not discuss ratings with peers.

1. The previous non-holder chooses their next ticket first.
2. They message the previous holder when their selection is complete.
